headline: The fastest ocean liner ever was sunk. On purpose.
summary: The SS United States crossed to Europe in three days in 1952 and still holds the record. It is longer than the Titanic. After nearly 30 years at a Philadelphia pier, a Florida county bought it, cut holes in the decks and opened the valves on Wednesday. No explosives. It now sits 180 feet down off Destin, the world's largest artificial reef.

cover_question.q: Why did they sink it on purpose?

cover_answer: Fish need homes too. It's a reef now, 180 feet down.
table_question: Save the old ship for looking at, or sink it for the fish?

5-7.script: A huge old ship called the SS United States was sunk on purpose in Florida on Wednesday. It is longer than the Titanic, and nobody was on board. Underwater it becomes a reef, a place where fish can live. Divers will go down to visit it.
5-7.why: A six-year-old knows the Titanic. One bigger ship, sunk on purpose with no one aboard, is the whole story.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole event, and the vivid feature here is a sinking ship. So the script says the thing they will worry about first: nobody was on board, and the grown-ups planned it. The Titanic is the measure because it is the one ship they know. Expect 'do the fish like it?' Yes, that is the point.

8-12.script: The SS United States crossed to Europe in three days in 1952 and still holds the record. Then jets came, and it lost money. It sat at a Philadelphia pier for nearly 30 years. A Florida county cut holes in its decks and opened the valves: no explosions, like pulling the plug on a bath.
8-12.why: A chain: jets, losses, 30 years at a pier, then a reef.
8-12.why_long: At ten they are working out chains of cause and effect, so the script hands over one: jets, losses, 30 years at a pier, then a county with a use for it. The bath plug is the mechanism: no explosion, just water in and the ship down. Expect 'why not just fix it up?' A museum and a floating hotel were both proposed, and both fell through.

13-17.script: Is a ship that carried Truman, Kennedy and Coco Chanel worth more as a museum or as a reef? The group that fought to save it lost; its president, whose grandfather helped design it, says she is glad the story lives on. Second: a county paid millions to sink it for divers. Keeping it, or burying it?
13-17.why: Two true things: a lost fight to save it, and a reef that keeps it.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things: the campaign to save this ship failed, and the people who ran it are glad about how it ended. The script asks them to weigh a museum nobody would fund against a reef divers will visit, and whether that counts as keeping something. Expect 'isn't this just dumping?' The county relies on over 500 reefs.

5-7.q: Why did they sink it on purpose?
5-7.a: It was too old to sail and nobody had room for it. Underwater it gives fish a home, so they let water in and it went down slowly.

8-12.q: Why didn't they make it a museum?
8-12.a: People tried for years. A museum and a hotel both fell through.

8-12.q: How do you sink a ship without blowing it up?
8-12.a: Cut holes in the decks and open the valves. Water floods in.

13-17.q: Why does a county want a sunken ship?
13-17.a: Sealife and paying divers. The county has over 500 reefs already.

13-17.q: Isn't that just dumping trash in the ocean?
13-17.a: It was cleaned in Alabama first, and no explosives were allowed.
